result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B is better. It treats wording, typo and formatting fixes differently from changes to steps, commands and versions, and it leaves names, time limits and channels as clear placeholders. A puts fixed day counts in the rule itself and never says which small edits can ship without a full review, though its requirement to run every step on a clean machine is strong. Both handle a reviewer who never answers well, but B's options to hold the changed steps or publish with a banner are more practical than A's override approach. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A is the better answer because it handles proportionality and placeholders better. It separates wording, typo and formatting fixes, which need only the owner's okay, from changed steps, commands and versions, which need a recorded run-through, and it leaves every name, time limit and channel as a clearly marked placeholder. B has a stronger testing requirement (a clean machine and a reviewer who can run the product) and a solid escalation path, but it treats every edit the same and puts specific day counts (3, 1 and 2 days, plus a 1-day fix target) into the rule text, mentioning only in a note that they can be changed.
